https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Maggie Eastland and Magan Crane
paragraphs: WASHINGTON — The US Commerce Department moved on Monday to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centers, significantly expanding export controls to close a critical cloud computing loophole.

Under the interim final rule issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US government is establishing mandatory export license requirements for transferring advanced semiconductors and cloud compute capacity to five intermediary nations: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.

The new regulation directly targets data centers and neocloud operators globally that provide high aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) computing power to entities headquartered in China or Macau. Existing facilities catering to these clients have been granted a 90-day grace period to apply for licenses and transition operations into compliance.

The aggressive policy shift comes as Washington intensifies scrutiny over how restricted American technology reaches Chinese tech giants despite sweeping hardware export restrictions. In recent months, reports revealed that companies in China had increasingly bypassed physical chip embargos by renting computing clusters running Nvidia Corp. H100 and H200 accelerators stationed across Southeast Asia.

Enforcement concerns escalated following the sudden departure of former Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, amid congressional inquiries into transactions with Singapore-based provider Megaspeed International. Megaspeed had imported billions of dollars worth of Nvidia hardware between 2023 and 2025, leasing high-performance clusters to overseas clients including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and ByteDance Ltd.

While renting cloud compute does not violate legacy rules restricted to physical hardware delivery, the Commerce Department determined that remote access effectively nullifies national security protections by enabling Chinese frontier labs to train advanced large language models using American supercomputing infrastructure.

Under the new framework, cloud providers must implement verified customer identity protocols and adhere to strict compute quotas. Global data center operators serving clients in designated restricted regions will be prohibited from dedicating more than 50% of aggregate cluster capacity to Chinese firms without explicit Commerce Department authorization.

The interim rule takes effect immediately with an open public comment period. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill welcomed the measure as an essential step toward hardening the semiconductor perimeter, with members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee indicating plans for oversight hearings on export control enforcement mechanisms.

paragraphs: Big Tech Mounts Last-Ditch Push to Rewrite Canada’s Data Access Bill Bloomberg · Photographer: Betty Laura Zapata/Bloomberg Laura Osman Mon, 16 November 2026 at 3:00 am GMT-8 5 min read (Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is facing fierce pushback from Big Tech firms over security legislation that would require companies to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement.

Lobbyists and executives from Meta Platforms Inc., Apple Inc. and Alphabet Inc. are mounting a last-ditch blitz in Ottawa to rewrite the bill before it passes. On Monday, leaders from Meta, Signal Messenger LLC and Tailscale Inc. will take their fight to a key Senate committee hearing that will shape the legislation's final form.

Bill C-22, so-called "lawful access" legislation, is designed to allow Canada's spy agency and police services to compel electronic service providers to preserve and turn over certain metadata. The government insists the measures simply align Canada with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven allies.

Tech firms, privacy advocates and US lawmakers counter that the bill goes far beyond frameworks adopted by Canada's peers, warning it would threaten platform security and user privacy. Meta has argued the law would effectively conscript its platforms as "an arm of the government's surveillance apparatus."

"There's a real possibility that both the security and the privacy of Canadian users of these systems is really undermined," Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy in Canada, said in an interview.

For Carney's government, the battle risks chilling tech investment, escalating tensions with the US and driving privacy-focused platforms out of the Canadian market. Signal has threatened to pull out of Canada if the bill passes in its current form. Proton AG, a Swiss tech firm, has said it would rethink its expansion plans in the country.

The bill's critics object to a rule that would let the government force electronic service providers to retain certain user metadata for up to six months so it can be disclosed to law enforcement officials, if needed.

The proposed law could also compel some firms to unlock encrypted data — but only if they built the encryption and possess the information necessary to unlock it. Earlier this year, lawmakers amended the bill to make clear that companies also cannot be forced to introduce a "systemic vulnerability" into their software.

Those guardrails were meant to ease fears from firms like Signal and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, that the bill targeted end-to-end encryption. That form of encryption ensures only the sender and receiver can read the messages — meaning the company doesn't have the ability to decrypt them.

Even so, privacy advocates and tech leaders argue that the bill still gives the government sweeping power to order firms to build "technical capabilities" to intercept communications and hand over data.

Tech companies have long warned they cannot create "backdoor" access only for law enforcement without weakening security for all users. Curran said an order that would make Meta's systems more vulnerable is a "red line" for the company, and likely its industry peers as well.
"It probably puts Canada in a position where there's going to eventually be a bit of a standoff between service providers and the government, and it's not good for Canadians," she said.

The UK and Apple faced a similar dispute last year when the government ordered the company to circumvent encryption that the company uses to secure user data stored on its cloud services. Apple challenged the order and removed its advanced data protection feature for British users. The case is still before the courts.
"In the hypothetical future, if we faced similar orders, we would have to consider those options," Curran said.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree has said the bill has already been amended to alleviate the concerns raised by Apple in the UK about the potential impact on encryption. He has accused some critics, including Big Tech companies, of spreading misinformation about the bill.

"Bill C-22 does not authorize indiscriminate surveillance and does not permit or compel companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called 'backdoors.' Any claims suggesting otherwise are incorrect," Simon Lafortune, the minister's spokesperson, said in a statement.

Apple said in a statement it appreciates the Canadian government's efforts to improve the bill, but the current version would still undermine the company's ability to offer privacy and security features, including encryption, "even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses."

US lawmakers have also pushed back. In May, Republican House Representatives Jim Jordan and Brian Mast warned in a letter to Anandasangaree that the bill would "create significant cross-border risks to the security and data privacy of Americans."

The Canadian Senate committee is the bill's last legislative hurdle before potential passage into law. While the appointed chamber rarely rejects bills outright, it frequently secures amendments — leaving tech giants and privacy advocates one last venue to lobby for changes.

Revenue for the three months ended September slid 1% to 30.8 billion yuan ($4.6 billion), in line with the average analyst forecast. Net income came in at 1.4 billion yuan.

China's internet search leader is trying to reclaim its place in a hotly contested AI arena where longtime rivals such as Tencent Holdings Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. have pulled ahead. Its Ernie model series has fallen out of the top tier and lags upstarts like DeepSeek and Moonshot, while its consumer AI products have yet to catch on. Compounding the slump, Baidu's main online advertising business is losing eyeballs and marketers to newer social apps.

Billionaire founder Robin Li is betting that a surge in autonomous AI agents will create a new ecosystem from which Baidu can reap returns on its cloud computing and chip infrastructure. Its AI-driven business now accounts for more than half of its top line, a trend the company expects to persist. The company last week unveiled a token marketplace that connects idle compute with developers hungry for open-source models — a move aimed at displacing middlemen, known as transfer stations, with accredited providers.

The resource-constrained company lacks the scale to compete with China's tech platforms and the strain is beginning to show as Baidu simultaneously pursues leadership in China's AI, cloud and robotaxi sectors. The potential spinoff and IPO of the Kunlunxin AI chip unit won't improve its earnings prospects, which are highly challenged.

Its chip spinoff Kunlunxin is gearing up for an independent listing in Hong Kong, setting up a showdown against Alibaba's T-Head, which announced a similar move. But Kunlunxin's market debut could slip to next year because of broader market weakness and China's tighter controls on AI funding, Bloomberg News has reported.
Baidu last week released its latest foundation model, Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview, which it positioned for fast inference speeds and competitive pricing.
In autonomous driving, Baidu's Apollo Go robotaxi service now spans more than a score of cities globally, including fully driverless commercial operations in Dubai.

The e-commerce giant-turned-AI player said its Qwen4-Max model scored near the top of coding benchmarks, outperforming Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 as well as homegrown rival Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro. Alibaba did not make the model open weight, which would allow users to download and customize it, but said it would make smaller versions of the series available soon.

paragraphs: By Kwanwoo Jun South Korean memory-chip giant SK Hynix plans to spend 1.4 trillion won, equivalent to $1.05 billion, over the next five years to support small local suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts and equipment, in order to strengthen the competitiveness of its supply chain.

As part of the plan, SK Hynix will open a semiconductor testing facility, jointly funded with about 875 billion won in investment, in May 2027 at its chip-making complex in Yongin, south of Seoul, the company said Monday. The facility now under construction, named Trinity Fab, is the result of a three-way partnership between SK Hynix, the central government and the Yongin municipal government, which have committed 443.2 billion won, 373.6 billion won and 57.7 billion won, respectively, the company said.

By sharing the facility, which will feature a large clean room and state-of-the-art testing equipment based on 12-inch wafers, domestic suppliers will be able to reduce the costs and time needed to bring their products to commercial production and market, it said. SK Hynix also plans to provide suppliers with technical and financial support, if needed, at the facility.

paragraphs: At the $74 midpoint, each founder's stake is worth roughly $17.8 billion to $18.1 billion before accounting for the shares they plan to sell in the offering. One cofounder, little known outside the company, owns more stock than CEO Dario Amodei. Large founder allocations are not unusual in Silicon Valley.

Snap's Evan Spiegel and Bobby Murphy, for example, retained enough super-voting stock to control about 89% of the voting power after the company's 2017 IPO. What makes Anthropic unique is the number of founders with huge stakes and how evenly those stakes are divided. Anthropic cofounder and Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown owns about 244 million shares of the AI startup, according to its S-1.

That narrowly tops the stakes of Anthropic's six other cofounders, who each own roughly 232 million to 243 million shares. At the $74 midpoint of Anthropic's expected IPO range, Brown's stake would be worth about $18.1 billion. The filing shows that Brown plans to sell 3.38 million shares in the offering, worth roughly $250 million at that price, leaving him with stock worth about $17.8 billion.

Brown co-founded Anthropic with the Amodei siblings and four others in January 2021. He now serves as chief compute officer, where he leads the technical organization responsible for "securing, scaling, and effectively using" Anthropic's computing resources, according to the filing.

Brown also played an important role in the technology that led to today's generative-AI boom. Before Anthropic, he worked at OpenAI, where the S-1 says he led the engineering of GPT-3. Brown and Dario Amodei also co-invented what Anthropic calls "deep RLHF," which the company said was central to transforming base large language models into conversational assistants such as Claude.

After Brown, Sam McCandlish has the next-largest disclosed stake, with about 243.4 million shares, worth roughly $18 billion at the midpoint. Christopher Olah holds about 242.9 million shares, followed by chief science officer Jared Kaplan with 242.4 million shares and Jack Clark with 242.3 million shares.

At the midpoint, their stakes are each worth about $17.9 billion before their planned IPO sales. Anthropic president Daniela Amodei owns 241.4 million shares, worth about $17.9 billion at the midpoint. CEO Dario Amodei owns 240.6 million shares, worth about $17.8 billion, and also controls voting proxies over another 4.6 million shares.

The founders' influence will extend far beyond their economic stakes. Immediately before the IPO, Anthropic plans to issue a special Class F share to an LLC controlled by the seven cofounders. That single share will carry 50.1% of Anthropic's total voting power on matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of directors other than those selected by Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust.

In another unusual twist, Anthropic says each of its cofounders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropic causes. Some of Silicon Valley's biggest companies and venture firms also stand to make huge windfalls from Anthropic's public-market debut.

Amazon and Google will each own more than 5% of Anthropic after the IPO conversions, making them two of the company’s largest strategic shareholders. At the midpoint of Anthropic's expected IPO range, Amazon's 1.92 billion shares would be worth about $142 billion, while Google's stake would be worth about $132 billion.

Among traditional venture firms, the filing provides unusually detailed numbers for Spark Capital because Spark partner Yasmin Razavi sits on Anthropic's board and was the first firm to invest when Anthropic was valued at $4.5 billion in 2023. Spark-affiliated funds have invested across at least six Anthropic financings since 2023.

Menlo Ventures led a round in 2024 when Anthropic was valued at about $18 billion. They have now invested over $1.3 billion in the company, also earning them a stake between 1.5% and 2%, according to a person familiar with the matter. Lightspeed Venture Partners is the largest venture shareholder, owning almost 2% of Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter.

They led a round at a $61.5 billion valuation in late 2024 and continued to double down. Iconiq also amassed a large stake by investing $6 billion in the company, according to a person familiar with the matter, giving the firm an ownership stake between 1.5% and 2%. Bessemer Venture Partners first invested in the Series D in 2024 and continued to write checks in every round since.

It has spent around $800 million on Anthropic, making it the firm's largest investment to date. Bessemer has an almost 1% stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter. Other major winners include Coatue, which has invested $4.75 billion, and Sound Ventures, which invested more than $400 million, according to people familiar with the matter.

Apple's latest tech move is HomeView, a smart-home hub designed to bring a more personalized version of Siri into consumers' homes. The device highlights Apple's continued push to make its AI assistant more useful across its ecosystem — the same broader technology that drew scrutiny in a class-action lawsuit over delayed Siri AI capabilities for iPhones.

Plaintiffs alleged that Apple's marketing created expectations about AI features that weren't available when consumers purchased their phones. Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle the class-action lawsuit, without admitting wrongdoing. The agreement is subject to judge approval.

Now, as Apple expands its AI ambitions to compete with Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub, consumers face a familiar question: Should they pay for another Apple device with its major selling point being AI?
Here's what to know about the new AI-powered tech, the ongoing lawsuit and how to claim your share of the pending settlement before it's too late.

Apple HomeView, which will retail at $299, is a smart home-management device that features a seven-inch Liquid Retina display touchscreen, a built-in speaker and a camera that recognizes individual household members, allowing it to personalize the experience for up to six people. Users can make FaceTime calls, play music, view security camera feeds and control connected devices such as thermostats, lights and smart locks, according to Apple's announcement.

But HomeView's biggest selling point is its integration with Apple Intelligence, the company's AI platform that also powers newer Siri capabilities. Apple's upgraded Siri is designed to do more than respond to basic voice commands. The assistant is expected to understand personal context, provide more conversational responses and use information from apps to help users complete tasks.

For example, users can ask questions that require information from their personal schedules rather than relying solely on general internet knowledge. When paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomeView can draw on information from apps such as iMessage and Calendar to deliver more personalized responses.

"Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user," Greg Joswiak, Apple's SVP of worldwide marketing, said in a statement. "It's powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone's information private and secure."
Apple HomeView, releasing on Nov. 13, leverages the same broader technology at the center of Apple's pending $250 million settlement.

While Apple denies all of the allegations made in the class-action lawsuit — customer claims centered on the company's 2024 unveiling of new AI-powered capabilities for Siri, including the ability to understand a user's personal context, recognize what's displayed on their screen and perform more actions across apps.

"Powered by Apple Intelligence, Siri becomes more deeply integrated into the system experience," the company wrote in a June 2024 press release introducing Apple Intelligence. "With richer language-understanding capabilities, Siri is more natural, more contextually relevant and more personal, with the ability to simplify and accelerate everyday tasks."

HomeView is not part of the aforementioned settlement. But the tech giant's broader push to develop Siri into a more capable, personalized AI assistant drives consumer interest in the device in the same way.
However, it's worth noting that to fully leverage HomeView, users will need to connect other Apple devices for a more personalized feel.

According to the court-filed motion for preliminary approval, filed on May 5, Apple's $250 million settlement agreement establishes a fund to compensate eligible U.S. consumers who have purchased an eligible device between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, for personal or business use rather than resale.
Eligible devices include the iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 15 Pro, and iPhone 15 Pro Max — of which there are approximately 37 million.

Consumers who submit valid claims by Dec. 21, 2026 may receive $25 per device, with payments potentially reaching $95 depending on the number of valid claims and other settlement costs, according to the official settlement website.

Some consumers may have received a settlement notice by email or in the mail containing a claim identification number and PIN. If you did not receive a notice, you can still file a claim by selecting, "I DO NOT have a Claim ID and PIN, but I would like to file a claim online" on the form.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.title: SpaceX Plans $24 Billion Data Center and Gas Plant in Texas
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: SpaceX plans to construct, own and operate a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility at its company town in Starbase, Texas, according to a notice of a public hearing on the city’s website.
The estimated investment for the initial phase of the project is $24 billion. The city commissioner will consider the approval of a tax abatement and development agreement at a Dec. 9 meeting.

The proposal is the latest sign that CEO Elon Musk is seeking to vertically integrate SpaceX’s value chain for natural gas, the primary power-plant fuel that data center developers are using to get the facilities up and running. SpaceX is also looking to fuel some of its rocket launches with a super-chilled and purified form of the gas.

In September, SpaceX proposed building its own pipeline in Florida to transport gas to its Starship rockets in Cape Canaveral. The company has also been hiring gas traders in Starbase and Cape Canaveral to support its growing fuel and power needs, rather than relying on external logistics companies.

Starbase, incorporated in 2025, is home to several hundred SpaceX employees and their families. The proposed project is located within the corporate limits of Starbase on a 444-acre tract east of the city of Brownsville, according to the public notice.

Surging power needs from data centers and new factories have driven demand for gas plants, and Musk has long been a proponent for vertical integration. SpaceX also plans to build its own gas-fired power plant to support the massive semiconductor manufacturing facility it’s developing in Grimes County, outside of Houston, with Tesla Inc.

Musk’s prospects for getting a “super-compute facility” and associated gas infrastructure online could face headwinds from Texas’ incoming Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa, who ran in part on a promise to tame new data center construction. Rising power prices and concerns around the environmental impact of the facilities have triggered protests around the country, including ones against SpaceXSI’s data center complex in Memphis.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.title: Binance’s CFO Leaves Company in Wake of $6 Billion Crypto Heist
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: Kaiser Ng, the chief financial officer at Binance Holdings Ltd., the world’s largest crypto exchange, is leaving, the company announced just days after hackers stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the platform.

“Kaiser Ng has decided to pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance, with a transition plan implemented over the last six months,” Binance co-Chief Executive Officer Yi He said in a statement. “We wish him the best in his next chapter.” Justin Yek will become the firm’s new CFO, she said.
Related: Binance $6.3 Billion Heist to Prompt Closer Scrutiny by Insurers

Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance last week in the biggest heist in cryptocurrency’s history. It came as the industry leapfrogs into the mainstream at a time when the ascent of artificial intelligence presents ever-increasing cybersecurity challenges.
Crypto exchanges Bitget, Bybit and other platforms have also suffered major hacks.

The FBI said on Oct. 31 that North Korea was responsible for the Binance attack. The exchange subsequently said it had covered about 90% of the $6.3 billion, making progress on its pledge to fully reimburse customers.

Ng joined the firm in January 2022, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before Binance, he was at Kraken, another crypto exchange, for about five years. Ng did not immediately respond to a request for comment via Linkedin.
Yek was most recently at payments platform Airwallex as vice-president of finance.

“I am thrilled to step into the role of CFO at Binance,” Yek said in the statement. “I look forward to leading our finance organization as we continue to scale responsibly and deliver on our mission globally.”

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.title: Samsung Joins Cuff-Shaped Earbuds Trend With $229 Galaxy Buds On
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: Samsung unveiled its first pair of cuff-style earbuds, adding to a growing category that includes products from Sony, Bose and several Chinese brands.

The $229 Galaxy Buds On, announced Wednesday, have a C-shaped appearance, also referred to as a “clip-on” design, which hugs the earlobe almost like an earring. The earbuds are designed to let people listen to music and other audio while remaining aware of their surroundings. Since they hug the lobe, the ear canal remains unobstructed, making ambient sounds easy to hear. The earbuds are available in black and will go on sale Nov. 6.

In a news briefing, Samsung said it developed the Galaxy Buds On through an AI-driven computational design process informed by over 119 million ear-data points, ultimately settling on an ergonomic fit that works across a diverse range of ear shapes.

The earbuds include tap controls and can be configured to automatically adjust the volume based on how loud the environment is. Sound leakage can sometimes be an issue with open-fit earphones, potentially disturbing people nearby. But Samsung said it took steps to keep listening sessions more private, including “projecting reversed sound waves from the rear of the speaker.”

The On earbuds have a dust and water resistance rating of IP54, meaning they can endure splashes but shouldn’t be fully submerged and aren’t recommended for poolside use or taking to the beach. Battery life is rated for 9.5 hours of continuous playback — the longest of any Galaxy Bud product to date, according to the company. That usage time is possible largely because the earbuds don’t include active noise cancellation, which drains power more quickly. Including top-offs from the charging case, they can last as long as 38 hours, Samsung said.

Like previous Galaxy Buds, the On model supports hands-free voice commands with Google’s Gemini assistant. Users can answer or dismiss calls with head gestures, while a long press activates Quick Voice Memo for recording a thought or to-do.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.title: Anduril and Qualcomm Plan to Build Laptop With US Supply Chain
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: Defense tech startup Anduril Industries Inc. has joined forces with chipmaker Qualcomm Inc. to produce laptops that are designed and assembled in the US, an attempt to rebuild a manufacturing process that has largely moved overseas.The companies unveiled a new product line on Tuesday called BlueChip intended to supply “America’s most critical industries — including government, defense, first responders and public safety,” according to a statement.

The eventual goal is to establish an “end-to-end American supply chain” for the laptops and, more broadly, to rebuild US computer manufacturing, the companies said.“The United States pioneered personal computing and continues to lead the world in designing advanced technology, but decades of offshoring have left America dependent on foreign manufacturers for the computers and components that power everything from personal devices to critical government infrastructure,” according to the statement.

“This dependence creates a national security vulnerability.”BlueChip laptops will be manufactured in the US, with circuit board assembly planned for Anduril’s sprawling Arsenal-1 defense manufacturing facility in Ohio. The Costa Mesa, California-based company manufactures drones, missiles and other defense technology.

Qualcomm, which is based in San Diego, will supply the laptop’s general-purpose processing, graphics and on-device artificial intelligence.Anduril founder Palmer Luckey said building an autonomous drone isn’t very different from building a computer. Both products have central processors and graphics chips, as well as “memory, storage, mainboard, battery, sensors, wireless radios — it’s basically all the same stuff,” he said.

“The only difference is the shape, and that it has a screen and a keyboard.”It’s become increasingly difficult for American technology companies to source critical parts in the US and allied countries, while still making products at competitive prices. Many of the key parts and raw materials in drones mostly come from China.“In the near term, this is going to be more expensive than a laptop made in China,” Luckey said.

“I am very optimistic about the long run that we’re going to be able to make computers here in America that are just as competitive.”He declined to provide production targets for the laptops, but he said they would be the first of many BlueChip products. Anduril has produced functional prototypes of the BlueChip laptop and will begin taking orders next year, according to the companies.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: DeepSeek and MiniMax Group Inc have won approval to deploy models overseas, part of a wave of homegrown AI technologies that Beijing will allow to operate globally, a Chinese state media affiliate said.

Much of Chinese AI will remain free for export, according to a post published by Yuyuantantian, a social account affiliated with state broadcaster China Central Television. It addressed Beijing’s draft proposal for export control measures that would restrict certain artificial intelligence (AI) tools and services, including large language models and agents.
The proposed restrictions could limit overseas access to China’s most advanced models, potentially slowing an international surge in adoption driven by cost-effective Chinese open-source AI.

"Since the policy was announced, leading companies DeepSeek and MiniMax have successfully completed the registration process, as well as the procedures for open-sourcing and authorising overseas use,” according to the post published late Thursday (Oct 22) by Yuyuantantian. "AI companies can continue their commercialisation efforts as usual.”

Chinese startups have made significant strides closing the gap on US market leaders this year. Beyond more affordable pricing, they’ve also attracted users by making their models easier to customise than proprietary systems like the ones on offer from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC.

Beijing’s interest in controlling the export of what’s seen as strategically important technology has shown up most prominently in the way it forced the unwinding of Meta Platforms Inc’s acquisition of Manus, an AI agent startup with Chinese roots.

China regularly updates its catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first administration of US President Donald Trump threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company.

The latest revisions have been in development since the first half of the year, with government departments consulting and integrating feedback from research institutions and industry participants, Yuyuantantian said. The post stressed that the catalogue aims to "define boundaries rather than simply restrict the export of AI technology.”

There are significant carveouts to the proposed regulations. Providing API access, web applications or software-as-a-service features will not be subject to export restrictions, even if powered by restricted underlying models, according to the post.
The post contrasted Beijing’s approach with that of Washington, accusing the US of using targeted export bans and technology blockades to protect its competitive dominance.
"China, however, is not following this path,” the post added. – Bloomberg

paragraphs: By Natasha Mascarenhas and Tom Maloney Former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt owns around 1% of Anthropic PBC thanks to his early investment in the startup, according to people familiar with the matter, setting him up for one of the largest individual windfalls from the company’s imminent public market debut.

Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic’s Series A fundraising round, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because they weren’t authorized to discuss private matters. It’s unclear if he has sold any part of his stake since the initial investment.

Schmidt and Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO is set to generate massive windfalls for its employees and investors. The startup’s seven co-founders are already worth $8 billion each based on its last funding round, fortunes that propelled them onto the Bloomberg Billionaires Index of the world’s 500 richest people.

When Schmidt, 71, made his first bet on Anthropic in 2021, it was valued at $461 million, according to data company Pitchbook. Investors indicated last week that a fair valuation for the company is in the $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion ballpark; the high end of that range would value Anthropic at more than 4,300 times its Series A funding round.

At that value, the Anthropic stake would boost Schmidt’s net worth by about one-third to nearly $80 billion, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. Even using Anthropic’s most recent valuation of $965 billion, Schmidt adds nearly $10 billion to his existing fortune of $57.5 billion.

Schmidt has become a prolific technology investor over the past decade and a half, across several investment platforms including TomorrowVentures, Innovation Endeavors and his Hillspire family office, which Pitchbook associates with hundreds of different venture capital bets. His early portfolio focused on consumer internet, software and financial technology, but more recently artificial intelligence has been a major focus, with investments in Mistral AI, Reflection AI and World Labs, as well as Anthropic.

If Anthropic’s public stock debuts at a $2 trillion value, his bet on the company would beat Innovation Endeavors’ own early bet on Uber Technologies Inc. in 2011. By the time that company went public in 2019, its value had increased about 1,400-fold to $82 billion. Anthropic is set to begin formally marketing its initial public offering as soon as the week of Nov. 9, putting it in line to begin trading before the US Thanksgiving holiday, people familiar with the matter said earlier this month.

It’s expected to make its debut no later than the end of the year. The startup’s major backers include Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., Nvidia Corp. and Microsoft Corp., which have all poured billions into the Claude chatbot maker. Venture firms Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital also each put more than $2 billion into the company when they led a $65 billion funding round in May that tipped Anthropic’s valuation higher than its rival OpenAI for the first time.
The company — whose other backers include Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital — expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s record-setting $1.77 trillion June IPO, people familiar have said.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/.author: Bloomberg News
paragraphs: Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds.

China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to tighten control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector.

The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds.

Chinese AI startups have in summer 2026 made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s latest editions offer better pricing and Chinese companies also favour the approach of sharing the weights – used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer – of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them.
They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI making their wares available on US cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services.

The proposal forms part of a broader effort to control 40 technologies across industries where Chinese companies have become increasingly competitive. It would also cover five biomedical technologies and 12 solar technologies, including proprietary cell and gene-therapy platforms and production technology for certain advanced solar modules.

“This is more than routine maintenance,” said Ryan Etzcorn, a senior director at Ankura China Advisors. “By targeting AI, solar and biotech – industries where China holds a growing edge – Beijing is signalling that steadier relations with the West do not mean it will stand still.”

China regularly updates its catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first Trump administration threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company.

The proposed AI export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of the technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities.

“The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models trained on “important data” and containing at least 2 trillion parameters – like Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max – or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety.
China’s cyberspace regulator broadly defines such data as information that, if leaked, may endanger national security, economic operation, social stability or public safety.

The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licencing regime and potential US sanctions. The proposed restrictions against shipping mega-parameter models abroad are likely to hamper development given AI labs are training ever larger platforms: in September, Alibaba declared plans to develop models with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, far larger than what’s common today, for longer and more complex tasks.

Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government will provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies.

Deploying a covered model overseas would constitute a technology export, according to a statement. Deployments on overseas infrastructure owned by the Chinese provider could qualify for automatic licencing.

Companies that allow overseas customers to use restricted AI models through apps, websites or online services would not be subject to the proposed controls, the Commerce Ministry said. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity.

The ministry also proposed to restrict the export of design technologies for AI chips built using 14-nanometer or more advanced techniques or employing 2.5D or 3D advanced packaging. The proposed restrictions also cover design technologies for certain advanced memory chips.

China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect on Oct 16 and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licencing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control. paragraphs: SHARE 15 1.0x 15 00:00 / 00:00 Ready Text to speech Jason Schreier’s latest comments put the GTA 6 online release date in late 2027, well after the base game arrives on November 19. That lines up with the current launch plan: players get the single-player campaign first, while the multiplayer piece remains a separate arrival.

Originals framed the timing in a video titled Why GTA 6 Took 13 Years and $1 Billion to Make. In the narration, the game that ships in 2026 is “not even its final form,” and “The real long-term engine arrives a year later with multiplayer.”

That is the clearest public hint yet that GTA 6 Online could land about a year after the base release. For players, it means launch planning should be split in two: one date for the campaign, another for the online mode that usually becomes the long-run revenue engine.

In August, Schreier said Take-Two and Rockstar were not planning to reveal details about the new GTA Online anytime soon. He later clarified that Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick had not specifically discussed when the multiplayer mode would launch.

That history matters because it shows how little firm timing has been put on the record. The late 2027 window comes from a narrator’s framing, not from a timetable released by Rockstar or Take-Two, so it reads more like a forecast than a formal schedule.

Rockstar and Take-Two have not officially confirmed the release window, which leaves November 19 as the only hard date in the rollout. The practical takeaway is simple: anyone waiting for GTA 6 Online should expect the base game first and a longer wait before multiplayer is in hand.
Until Rockstar or Take-Two puts a date on the multiplayer mode, late 2027 is the most concrete outside estimate on the table — useful, but still an estimate.

In August, Schreier said Take-Two and Rockstar were not planning to reveal details about the new GTA Online anytime soon. He later clarified that Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick had not specifically discussed when the multiplayer mode would launch.

That history matters because it shows how little firm timing has been put on the record. The late 2027 window comes from a narrator’s framing, not from a timetable released by Rockstar or Take-Two, so it reads more like a forecast than a formal schedule.

paragraphs: Anthropic PBC is seeking to go public as soon as the middle of November, according to people familiar with the matter, after the artificial intelligence model maker pushed back plans to list. The firm behind Claude could start formal marketing for its IPO as soon as the week of Nov. 9, putting it in line to begin trading before Thanksgiving, the people said.

Dealmaking typically grinds to a halt in the days around the holiday, which is on Nov. 26. Anthropic is still expected to make its debut no later than the end of the year, the people said. The AI developer had been poised to file publicly for an initial public offering after the summer, Bloomberg News has reported.

Deliberations are ongoing and the timeline could continue to shift, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Anthropic, ascendant for much of this year, now faces renewed competition from the likes of OpenAI, which has gained sales momentum in recent months.

The companies are also at the center of mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, ramping up concern about the potential impact on Anthropic’s market debut. Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei published an essay on his personal website arguing the speed at which new AI models are advancing must be slowed down.

OpenAI, a chief rival to Anthropic, has postponed its IPO plans, with CEO Sam Altman arguing it’d be ill-advised to go public now. The concern doesn’t appear to have discouraged prospective investors, who believe a fair valuation for Anthropic is in the $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion ballpark, some of the people said.

The company expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, Bloomberg News has reported. Anthropic had a net loss of almost $42 billion in 2025, a roughly fivefold increase from about $8.3 billion the year before, Bloomberg News reported in August. The company’s full-year revenue was roughly $4.6 billion for 2025, up markedly from $386 million in the year before, though its operating loss ballooned to more than $8 billion, according to documents seen by Bloomberg News.

The bulk of the net loss was driven by a jump in the change in fair value of Anthropic’s liabilities which accounted for more than $34 billion of the company’s annual losses, the documents show. Reuters reported some details of the IPO valuation and financials previously. A representative for Anthropic couldn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Powering ahead with an IPO would see Anthropic defy the string of delays and postponements in the market for new listings. Oura Inc. was the third company in a matter of weeks to formally postpone its debut just hours before a planned first-time share sale, after some potential buyers balked at a fully diluted valuation target of about $15 billion.

A range of other companies have seen their targeted timelines slip as the performance for this year’s class of IPOs stumbled. When removing SpaceX and SK Hynix Inc.’s record-setting listings, the weighted-average return for the more than 100 newly listed stocks is a loss of 4%, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

The figure sharply lags a 12% return for the S&P 500 Index and a 20% gain for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this year. --With assistance from Shirin Ghaffary and Dina Bass. More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com https://www.bloomberg.com/ ©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

paragraphs: Crypto services company Blockchain.com aims to go public this year, raise about $500 million in the initial public offering and secure a valuation of between $4 billion and $6 billion in the listing, Bloomberg reported Monday (Sept. 28), citing unnamed sources.
Blockchain.com is in talks with potential investors, and the details could change. The company declined Bloomberg’s request for comment, according to the report.
Blockchain.com announced in May that it had confidentially submitted a draft registration statement on Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission for an IPO.

“The number of shares to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering have not yet been determined,” the company said at the time in a press release. “The initial public offering is subject to market and other conditions and the completion of the SEC’s review process.”

Blockchain.com announced in November 2023 that it raised $110 million in a Series E funding round. Bloomberg reported at the time that the financing valued Blockchain.com at less than half the $14 billion it reached in 2022. That drop followed a downturn in the crypto market.

According to Monday’s Bloomberg report, the claims about Blockchain.com’s plans for an IPO come at a time when the crypto market appears to be recovering after the price of bitcoin began plummeting about a year ago. Since mid-August, bitcoin is up 33%.
Crypto company listings came to a stop when bitcoin prices fell, the report said.
Kraken parent Payward is considering going public, though its plans have slowed and its debut may not arrive until 2027, per the report.

Meanwhile, Blockchain.com and NYSE announced Sept. 23 that they signed a memorandum of understanding to enable Blockchain.com users to get access to tokenized U.S. exchange-listed equities and exchange-traded funds on the NYSE’s upcoming digital alternative trading system. The companies said the distribution plan is subject to regulatory approvals.

Peter Smith, executive chairman, CEO and co-founder of Blockchain.com, said at the time in a press release that people should have greater access to stock ownership, that tokenized stocks are a catalyst for greater economic freedom and that the collaboration will enable tens of millions of Blockchain.com users around the world to invest in these digital assets.

paragraphs: Jensen Huang helped power the AI boom. But can the industry keep moving without him at Nvidia?

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes it can. Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event in San Francisco, Altman said the artificial intelligence industry would be “fine” without Huang leading Nvidia.

He also acknowledged the former CEO’s extraordinary contribution to the sector, calling him a hero while adding that “heroes have flaws”. The comments mark Altman’s first public comments on Huang’s sudden resignation from Nvidia last week.
They come at a time when the chipmaker’s leadership transition has raised questions about the future of a company central to the global AI ecosystem.

OpenAI's CEO said it was difficult to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen Huang and the company he built. Nvidia’s graphics processing units, or GPUs, have become essential for training and running large AI models, making the company a critical supplier to OpenAI and other AI firms.
However, Sam Altman stopped short of saying whether Huang should return to the company. Asked about the possibility, he said he did not know enough to answer.

His response acknowledged Huang’s influence without taking a position on Nvidia’s internal leadership decisions. Altman also expressed empathy for Huang, drawing a parallel with his own removal from OpenAI by its board in 2023.

Jensen Huang resigned after reports of extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman who is not related to him and is reportedly suspected by US officials of passing information to Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia appointed its Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. The transition matters because Nvidia has become more than a chip supplier to the AI industry.
OpenAI and Nvidia have developed a close relationship over the past decade, spanning chips, data centres and financing.

Nvidia has also agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion to support OpenAI’s new data centre project in Ohio, according to the report. Asked whether he was concerned about Nvidia honouring its commitments after Huang’s departure, Altman said he was not.
He described Nvidia as a “behemoth of a company” and said people continued to trust its financial guarantees.
Who will succeed Jensen Huang? The race to find Nvidia's next chief begins

Huang’s exit has unsettled parts of Silicon Valley. Some technology executives and investors fear Nvidia could become more cautious about the large financial commitments that have helped fund the AI boom.

A campaign urging the company’s board to reinstate Huang has also attracted support from prominent industry figures. Sam Altman, however, pointed to the strength of demand and revenue across AI products.
He said the industry was growing strongly enough to withstand the uncertainty around Nvidia’s leadership.
His words do not diminish Jensen Huang’s role in building the AI ecosystem. Instead, they point to a distinction between the influence of one leader and the momentum of an entire industry.
Nvidia’s next chapter will show whether the company can maintain its pace without the person who led it for decades.

paragraphs: Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The news was first announced via an emailed press release sent out by Apple’s communications team in India early on Tuesday. The update rolled out in the U.S. and other markets later in the day.

The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.

Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.

With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the stand-alone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.

Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.

When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.

Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.

Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.

This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.

At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning.

Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.

Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.

The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.

The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.

To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards.)
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.

Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.

paragraphs: PORTLAND, Ore., Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Facteus, a provider of decision-grade economic intelligence built on US consumer transaction data, today announced that its consumer transaction insights are now available on ALTD , a leading alternative data analytics solution on the Bloomberg Terminal providing near real-time actionable insights and more than 5,000 KPI estimates that enable users to nowcast company-reported metrics.

Joining datasets spanning consumer transactions, foot and web traffic, mobile app insights, and healthcare prescriptions, Facteus is the newest consumer transaction data provider to make its insights available via the Terminal. The addition gives investment professionals a broader view of observed consumer spending trends, enabling them to corroborate signals and gain a deeper, more comprehensive view of company performance, directly within their investment research workflows.

Users can access a 14-day lagged view of Facteus' forecasting signal with visibility into revenue KPI trends, updated daily by 6AM ET. With Data Entitlements in ALTD , buyside firms contracted and permissioned directly through Facteus can access a 2-day lagged version of the same signals with additional granularity, enabling analysts and portfolio managers to monitor spend trends for the companies they cover with a two-day lag, alongside pricing, consensus estimates and news, without ever leaving the Terminal.

"Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity, yet most of the data investors rely on to track it has historically arrived weeks or months after the fact, through company disclosures and government releases," said Chris Marsh, CEO at Facteus. "Making Facteus data available on the Bloomberg Terminal puts our observed consumer spending trends directly into one of the investment community's most important workflows. It makes the signal easier to access, while giving firms that need greater speed, depth and granularity a path into the broader Facteus intelligence environment."

Consumer transaction data analytics provides investment teams with an additional lens into company performance between traditional financial reporting periods. By analyzing observed credit and debit card spend, investors can monitor changes in consumer demand, compare trends across companies, and identify shifts that may warrant deeper research.

Facteus transforms consumer transaction activity into company-level KPI estimates designed for investment analysis. Its availability through Bloomberg allows investors to incorporate those signals alongside a growing portfolio of high-quality alternative datasets, as well as the traditional financial, market and company information already available on the Terminal.

"Alternative data is most useful when investors can compare signals across multiple sources and evaluate them directly alongside a broader range of financial information such as broker research, estimates and news," said Richard Lai, Global Head of Company Financial and Alternative Data at Bloomberg. "Facteus adds another trusted view of US consumer transaction activity to ALTD , helping clients validate trends and add greater depth to company research and investment analysis."

Facteus turns the daily spending of the U.S. economy into decision-grade intelligence for Wall Street's top firms, America's favorite brands, and the agencies that power them. Using passively observed, privacy-safe transaction data sourced directly from more than 18 banking, financial services, and fintech partners, paired with years of robust data science ensuring representativeness, Facteus delivers a continuous, verified read on real economic behavior – from the national economy to a single store. The company validates its signal daily against BEA Personal Consumption Expenditures, U.S. Census Monthly Retail Sales, and company-reported earnings, giving clients a faster signal they can measure against the economy itself and act on before the market does. For more information, visit facteus.com or request a demo.

Trusted by the world's most influential decision-makers, the Terminal provides real-time access to news, data, insights and trading tools that help our customers turn knowledge into action.

Bloomberg is a global leader in business and financial information, delivering trusted data, news, and insights that bring transparency, efficiency, and fairness to markets.
